articles.title: Here’s Why Tennis Balls Come in Sealed Cans … but Footballs and Baseballs Don’t
articles.content:
The U.S. Open is underway in New York, and once again I’m reminded that I should have practiced harder when I was a junior. But bygones! Let’s talk tennis balls. Specifically, the ones that come sealed in pop-top cans.
If you didn’t know, not all of them do. “There are two types of tennis ball: pressureless and pressurized,” says Rod Cross, a retired physics professor and an expert on the technology of tennis. (The name of one of his books is The Physics and Technology of Tennis.) It’s the pressurized ones that come in cans, and coming up, he’ll explain why.
But wait … footballs are pressurized, which just means that the air pressure inside the ball is higher than outside. So are basketballs. And volleyballs. And tons of other sports balls. But hardly any of them are sold in cans. To further the tennis-ball conundrum: “In the old days, when I was young, even pressurized balls were sold in cardboard boxes, [not cans],” Cross says.
It’s all too much for this weekend warrior. What happened in the tennis-ball-packaging world since the professor was a kid? The balls haven’t changed all that much. Ahead, Cross explains why tennis balls come in cans and lets us in on a few secrets of the science of tennis balls. Read on to learn more.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, entertainment, cleaning, humor, travel and tech all week long.
It’s been nearly 100 years. When lawn tennis was established in the United States, starting around 1880, tennis balls were mostly sold in paper bags or cardboard boxes. In the late 1920s, the Pennsylvania Rubber Company, which later evolved into one of the biggest names in tennis, Penn, began selling tennis balls in sealed metal cans.
They came with a key that rolled back the top like a sardine can, and they could not be resealed. According to the International Tennis Hall of Fame, World War II’s metal shortages brought back cardboard for a while, and Cross remembers seeing them packed in boxes into the 1950s (the aforementioned “old days”).
Resealable lids came along in the 1950s and ’60s, and in 1972, pop-tops replaced the key. In the 1980s, companies switched to plastic cans.
Sealed cans allow manufacturers to control the pressure precisely inside the can, keeping tennis balls at their peak performance level for as long as possible. Here’s why using a can works best.
Pressurized tennis balls bounce because the air inside the ball is at a higher pressure than the outside atmosphere. As the ball hits your racket or the court, the pressurized air inside pushes against the rubber and helps it resist deformation (aka getting squashed), and the ball bounces.
“Normal atmospheric pressure is 14.7 psi, but the pressure inside the ball is about 27 to 29 psi,” Cross says. So sealing the can and injecting air under pressure keeps the balls in the exact environment they need to properly bounce. You can test this: Regulation hard-court tennis balls (called Type 2 or medium) must bounce back to between 53 and 58 inches when dropped from a height of 100 inches.
“Pressurized balls are sold in a pressured can to prevent the air from gradually leaking out through the porous rubber wall,” Cross says. Tennis balls have a hollow rubber core that is not airtight, and once that rubber core is formed and covered with fuzz, that’s it—there’s no way to pump them up like you can a football or soccer ball.
This is why pressureless balls, which bounce due to their thicker, stiffer rubber instead of an air-pressure differential, are popular for practice and in ball machines. “Pressureless balls last longer, since the air doesn’t leak out,” Cross says.
Sealed cans keep tennis balls fresher longer. Since a pressurized tennis ball loses air gradually, the old way of packing them in cardboard meant that by the time the balls arrived at the pro shop or sporting-goods store, they were already losing air and bounce. Players had to do a squeeze test to find good ones rather than have confidence that fresh balls were, well, fresh.
Today, that’s not a worry. Example: I have a few unopened cans of tennis balls in my garage. I bought a case months ago, and these are the stragglers. But I’m not worried in the least that they’ll be bad when I get to them. We’ll get to the specifics in the next section, but no matter how long it is, they’ll be infinitely more playable than if they had been sitting loose or in a cardboard box.
The Penn balls in my garage don’t have expiration dates, and I can’t find any indication that Wilsons do either. (Wilson is another big name in tennis.) So I suppose they could last indefinitely. But most tennis pros put the window of freshness on an unopened can at anywhere from six months to a year, with two years being the outside limit.
But after you crack it open, the countdown begins. “Once opened, balls in pressurized cans can still be used a few weeks later,” Cross says. But you won’t catch a pro using a three-week-old ball at Wimbledon. Those are more for you and me hitting around on a Sunday morning. Even then, after a few hard-play sessions, you’re going to notice a difference in the feel of the ball.
“At amateur-competition level, new balls are used for each morning or afternoon event, while at professional level, new balls are used after every nine games,” Cross says. As the ball gets smacked around, the felt cover gets fluffy and slows down the ball as it flies through the air. “That’s why professionals take three balls to serve, then throw away the most fluffy ball,” he adds.
That distinctive whoosh (which is always accompanied by that fresh tennis-ball smell) is the sound of the pressure being released from inside the can. As soon as you pop the top, the higher-pressure air inside the can rushes through the opening to the lower-pressure outside, creating sound waves that dissipate as the opening gets larger.
Yes. It won’t make it as good as new, but depending on your standards, it might be close enough. “Old balls can be repressurized by placing them in a pressurized container for a few days, but the outer felt cover will still be fluffy or worn down,” Cross says.
You can find basic pressurizers for less than $20 at Target and Tennis Warehouse, and more sophisticated versions online for about $75 and up.
No. “Pressureless balls are sold in a cardboard box,” Cross says. Since the air inside them is at regular atmospheric pressure, there’s no need to keep them in a pressurized can. You can also buy pressureless tennis balls in mesh bags, especially if you purchase in bulk.
Pressureless tennis balls were patented by Swedish shoe giant Tretorn in 1955, and Cross says they’re popular in Europe and South America. But we’re seeing more of them over here too. Due to environmental concerns over the use of plastic in pressurized tennis ball cans, Wilson developed a new pressureless ball called Triniti that mimics the livelier bounce, faster play and lighter “feel” of pressurized balls. These are sold in recyclable cardboard boxes.
Some do, but not many, and the reason is simple: “Other balls can be pumped up to the correct pressure with an air pump,” Cross says, though some balls don’t use air or pressure at all. Here’s how it breaks down.

How long have tennis balls come in cans?

So why do tennis balls come in sealed cans?

Sealed cans allow manufacturers to control the pressure precisely inside the can, keeping tennis balls at their peak performance level for as long as possible. Here’s why using a can works best.

It keeps them bouncy

Pressurized tennis balls bounce because the air inside the ball is at a higher pressure than the outside atmosphere. As the ball hits your racket or the court, the pressurized air inside pushes against the rubber and helps it resist deformation (aka getting squashed), and the ball bounces.

“Normal atmospheric pressure is 14.7 psi, but the pressure inside the ball is about 27 to 29 psi,” Cross says. You can test this: Regulation hard-court tennis balls (called Type 2 or medium) must bounce back to between 53 and 58 inches when dropped from a height of 100 inches.

Tennis balls have a hollow rubber core that is not airtight, and once that rubber core is formed and covered with fuzz, that’s it—there’s no way to pump them up like you can a football or soccer ball.

This is why pressureless balls, which bounce due to their thicker, stiffer rubber instead of an air-pressure differential, are popular for practice and in ball machines. “Pressureless balls last longer, since the air doesn’t leak out,” Cross says.

It preserves shelf life

Sealed cans keep tennis balls fresher longer. Since a pressurized tennis ball loses air gradually, the old way of packing them in cardboard meant that by the time the balls arrived at the pro shop or sporting-goods store, they were already losing air and bounce. Players had to do a squeeze test to find good ones rather than have confidence that fresh balls were, well, fresh.

Today, that’s not a worry. Example: I have a few unopened cans of tennis balls in my garage. I bought a case months ago, and these are the stragglers. But I’m not worried in the least that they’ll be bad when I get to them. We’ll get to the specifics in the next section, but no matter how long it is, they’ll be infinitely more playable than if they had been sitting loose or in a cardboard box.

How long can they last in there?

The Penn balls in my garage don’t have expiration dates, and I can’t find any indication that Wilsons do either. (Wilson is another big name in tennis.) So I suppose they could last indefinitely. But most tennis pros put the window of freshness on an unopened can at anywhere from six months to a year, with two years being the outside limit.

But after you crack it open, the countdown begins. “Once opened, balls in pressurized cans can still be used a few weeks later,” Cross says. But you won’t catch a pro using a three-week-old ball at Wimbledon. Those are more for you and me hitting around on a Sunday morning. Even then, after a few hard-play sessions, you’re going to notice a difference in the feel of the ball.

“At amateur-competition level, new balls are used for each morning or afternoon event, while at professional level, new balls are used after every nine games,” Cross says. As the ball gets smacked around, the felt cover gets fluffy and slows down the ball as it flies through the air. “That’s why professionals take three balls to serve, then throw away the most fluffy ball,” he adds.

What is that “psssshhh” sound that you hear when you open a can of tennis balls?

That distinctive whoosh (which is always accompanied by that fresh tennis-ball smell) is the sound of the pressure being released from inside the can. As soon as you pop the top, the higher-pressure air inside the can rushes through the opening to the lower-pressure outside, creating sound waves that dissipate as the opening gets larger.

Can you revive a tennis ball?

Yes. It won’t make it as good as new, but depending on your standards, it might be close enough. “Old balls can be repressurized by placing them in a pressurized container for a few days, but the outer felt cover will still be fluffy or worn down,” Cross says.

You can find basic pressurizers for less than $20 at Target and Tennis Warehouse, and more sophisticated versions online for about $75 and up.

Do all tennis balls come in cans?

No. “Pressureless balls are sold in a cardboard box,” Cross says. Since the air inside them is at regular atmospheric pressure, there’s no need to keep them in a pressurized can. You can also buy pressureless tennis balls in mesh bags, especially if you purchase in bulk.

Pressureless tennis balls were patented by Swedish shoe giant Tretorn in 1955, and Cross says they’re popular in Europe and South America. But we’re seeing more of them over here too. Due to environmental concerns over the use of plastic in pressurized tennis ball cans, Wilson developed a new pressureless ball called Triniti that mimics the livelier bounce, faster play and lighter “feel” of pressurized balls. These are sold in recyclable cardboard boxes.

Do other balls come in cans?

Some do, but not many, and the reason is simple: “Other balls can be pumped up to the correct pressure with an air pump,” Cross says, though some balls don’t use air or pressure at all. Here’s how it breaks down.

  • Padel balls: A very close cousin to the tennis ball, padel balls also have a hollow rubber core and a felt cover. They are sold under pressure in pop-top cans, but they are softer and have more give.
  • Racquetballs: The hollow, air-filled racquetball gets its bounce from the rubber shell, not the air inside (much like a pressureless tennis ball). So while they are often sold in cans to keep the rubber fresh, the cans are not pressurized.
  • Pickleballs: The nemesis of tennis players everywhere (I kid, pickleballers!), the plastic, Whiffle ball–like pickleball is hollow and has multiple holes, so it’s just sold in bags, boxes or other non-pressurized containers.
  • Footballs, soccer balls and basketballs: Larger air-filled balls are sold naked or in boxes and are filled using a bicycle pump or air compressor. (If you’ve ever searched your garage and junk drawers for hours looking for the pump’s needle attachment, you feel my pain.) These balls will eventually deflate, but give them a quick pump and you’ll be good to go.
  • Baseballs and golf balls: Solid-core balls do not have air inside at all, so there’s no need to sell or store them under pressure. They may get old and brittle, or lose performance capability after years of storage or use, but these balls won’t deflate.

articles.title: Watch The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview with Author Marlon James
articles.content: Marlon James is one of those rare authors who can do just about anything. Over the course of his career, the Jamaican novelist has taken readers from a remote village in 1950s Jamaica with John Crow’s Devil to a brutal sugar plantation during slavery in The Book of Night Women to the turbulent world surrounding the attempted assassination of Bob Marley in his Man Booker Prize–winning masterpiece, A Brief History of Seven Killings. He even co-hosts the literary podcast Marlon and Jake Read Dead People, and reinvented epic fantasy with his Dark Star trilogy. In other words: Trying to predict what James will do next is usually a losing game. His latest novel, The Disappearers, may be his most ambitious yet—and the acclaim has already been extraordinary, with the New York Times recently calling it “the novel of the decade, if not the century.” The sweeping epic follows the lives of eight gay men in Jamaica throughout the 1980s and ’90s, as they navigate love, loss and life in a world that criminalizes their identity. But don’t expect James to put it neatly into one box. “You can look at it as a revenge thriller, which it is,” he tells us. “You can [also] look at it as a story about longing, becoming, family and community, which it is.” And if our escalator interview is your first time meeting James off the page, prepare to be delighted. For someone responsible for some of the most powerful and complex novels of the past two decades, he’s refreshingly funny, wildly personable and full of unexpected opinions. One minute, he’s discussing literature and craft; the next, he’s talking about comfort reads, comic books and why superhero fans should absolutely know about his current obsession: Absolute Batman. For this episode of The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview, Leigh Belz Ray caught up with James at Barnes & Noble Union Square in New York City to talk about The Disappearers, his reading habits, his literary heroes and plenty more. Trust us—you’ll come away with a longer TBR list and an even greater appreciation for one of the most fascinating voices in contemporary fiction. Watch the exclusive interview with Marlon James below, and then scroll down to shop his books and reading recommendations! Through Fiction Favorites (formerly Select Editions and Condensed Books), Reader’s Digest has been publishing anthologies of abridged novels for decades. We’ve worked with some of the biggest names in fiction, including James Patterson, Ruth Ware, Kristin Hannah and more. The Reader’s Digest Book Club, helmed by Books Editor Tracey Neithercott, introduces readers to even more of today’s best fiction by upcoming, bestselling and award-winning authors. articles.title: Is It Really Rude to Ask People to Take Off Their Shoes When They Come into Your House?
articles.content:
Forget arguing about politics. A real high-stakes debate in American homes is about wearing shoes indoors. And there are some big differences by state. From Seattle to Arizona to Utah, people all have their own unique ways of treating the shoes-in-the-house question. One even involves checking for baby scorpions with a blacklight. (Looking at you, Phoenix.)
But Minnesota has the strictest policy I’ve personally encountered: Everyone takes off their shoes inside a home—every time, always. It was so well enforced that I became acutely aware of always wearing clean, non-holey socks because I knew people were going to see them. Now I live in Colorado, where people wear hiking shoes to weddings (to be fair, a lot of weddings here are in the mountains) and Tevas are considered an extension of your feet. Almost no one takes off their shoes inside a house unless they’re very wet or muddy.
But perhaps the biggest debate is in my own home. My husband and I have been bickering about this for years and still can’t come to a conclusion. (Well, I’m right, obviously, but I need your help convincing him.) I personally think Minnesota has the right idea. My husband not only thinks I’m nuts but also gets embarrassed when I ask guests—politely!—to remove their shoes. He says I’m being rude by asking them to take off a piece of personal clothing, so as a form of protest, he refuses to remove his shoes inside our home, not even after gardening and/or accidentally stepping on the dog. It’s become a whole thing.
So let’s save my marriage and my sanity and figure this out together. Putting aside familial power struggles, is it actually rude to ask people to take off their shoes when they come into your house?
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, home, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
I’m going to drop this first: All shoe soles showed contamination with microbes, including bacteria, fungi and fecal matter, in a 2023 study published in Indoor and Built Environment. And all of these germs transferred indoors when the shoe-wearing psychopath—er, I mean, person—walked inside. The majority of the germs were concentrated in the entryway, but carpet was an especially big magnet for gross stuff. So even if your shoes look clean, they’re about as clean as the dirty restroom floor you walked on earlier. Would you want that public bathroom floor in your home? No? Then the researchers recommend taking off your shoes.
“Taking off your shoes is a no-brainer,” said lead author Alessandra Leri, PhD, in an interview with Smithsonian Magazine.
So, yes, my argument is: Scientists say so. A lot of other people say so too. According to a 2023 CBS News/YouGov survey, two out of three Americans say they take off their shoes in their own home.
There’s also the practical case. Lots of things get tracked in via shoes—including mud, dirt, leaves, water, snow, ice and neon-green sidewalk chalk (ask me how I know)—that would require you to mop your floors.
And finally, there is the foot-stepping problem. Because my husband constantly wears shoes in the house, and the shoes reduce his ability to feel where he is stepping, he constantly steps on my toes, the kids’ toes and, occasionally, the poor dog. (The cat is faster and apparently smarter than the rest of us.)
OK, so that survey stat I just smugly dropped? While it’s true that two-thirds of Americans take off their shoes in their own homes, two-thirds of those folks said they don’t require guests to do the same. My husband is correct that most folks won’t ask guests to remove their shoes. But is that because it’s rude to ask or just because it’s kinda awkward? The overwhelming majority of poll respondents, 90%, did say they wouldn’t consider it an unreasonable request if asked to remove their shoes by a host.
I think what my husband is really getting at is that we often treat guests with a higher standard than we do ourselves, so when I ask people to please take off their shoes, it can come across as unwelcoming or uninviting. Maybe even a little patronizing? And this is especially true for people you may not know as well. It’s one thing to ask your sister to take off her shoes; it’s an entirely different story if you’re asking your boss who dropped by.
Then there’s the embarrassment factor, and it’s real. I had an almost pathological obsession with having new, clean and adorable socks on at all times when we lived in Minnesota, and the times I forgot, I was embarrassed. And it’s not just socks. Guests may be embarrassed by foot odor, lack of a pedicure, a medical condition or just weird-looking toes. (It’s my personal opinion that all toes are weird-looking, but whatever.)
Also, some people build their whole outfit around their shoes, and I am occasionally that person. A cute summer dress just isn’t as cute without the strappy heels, right? Asking someone to remove their shoes messes up the whole look—which isn’t a big deal for a casual visit but can be an issue if you’re meeting your son’s girlfriend’s parents for the first time.
As for the germs? Mopping isn’t really that hard. I hate it, but on the list of terrible chores, it’s not as awful as cleaning the toilet and maybe around the same level of annoying as wiping fingerprints off the stainless steel fridge. And it works: Mopping removes about 80% of tracked-in bacteria, while disinfecting gets rid of 95% to 99%, according to one study.
This isn’t solely (ha!) a cut-and-dry issue. And the more I think about it, the more middle ground I find. Here’s what to consider before setting a “shoes off” policy in your house.
You accept it. Ultimately, it’s their body. This is not the hill to die on: In the grand scheme of things, this is small stakes. This is how you keep friends. This is also how I’m still married.
It is not rude to ask someone to take off their shoes in your home—as long as you ask politely, offer options, are mindful of the situation and are ready to accept “no” as an answer. It doesn’t mean you have to be thrilled about it. And you are welcome to think vengeful thoughts as you mop the floor for the third time as your husband sits on the couch with his hiking shoes on, eating popcorn and smugly enjoying his shoe-wearing victory.

I’m going to drop this first: All shoe soles showed contamination with microbes, including bacteria, fungi and fecal matter, in a 2023 study published in Indoor and Built Environment. And all of these germs transferred indoors when the shoe-wearing psychopath—er, I mean, person—walked inside. The majority of the germs were concentrated in the entryway, but carpet was an especially big magnet for gross stuff. So even if your shoes look clean, they’re about as clean as the dirty restroom floor you walked on earlier. Would you want that public bathroom floor in your home? No? Then the researchers recommend taking off your shoes.

“Taking off your shoes is a no-brainer,” said lead author Alessandra Leri, PhD, in an interview with Smithsonian Magazine.

So, yes, my argument is: Scientists say so. A lot of other people say so too. According to a 2023 CBS News/YouGov survey, two out of three Americans say they take off their shoes in their own home.

There’s also the practical case. Lots of things get tracked in via shoes—including mud, dirt, leaves, water, snow, ice and neon-green sidewalk chalk (ask me how I know)—that would require you to mop your floors.

And finally, there is the foot-stepping problem. Because my husband constantly wears shoes in the house, and the shoes reduce his ability to feel where he is stepping, he constantly steps on my toes, the kids’ toes and, occasionally, the poor dog. (The cat is faster and apparently smarter than the rest of us.)

The case against asking guests to remove their shoes

OK, so that survey stat I just smugly dropped? While it’s true that two-thirds of Americans take off their shoes in their own homes, two-thirds of those folks said they don’t require guests to do the same. My husband is correct that most folks won’t ask guests to remove their shoes. But is that because it’s rude to ask or just because it’s kinda awkward? The overwhelming majority of poll respondents, 90%, did say they wouldn’t consider it an unreasonable request if asked to remove their shoes by a host.

I think what my husband is really getting at is that we often treat guests with a higher standard than we do ourselves, so when I ask people to please take off their shoes, it can come across as unwelcoming or uninviting. Maybe even a little patronizing? And this is especially true for people you may not know as well. It’s one thing to ask your sister to take off her shoes; it’s an entirely different story if you’re asking your boss who dropped by.

Then there’s the embarrassment factor, and it’s real. I had an almost pathological obsession with having new, clean and adorable socks on at all times when we lived in Minnesota, and the times I forgot, I was embarrassed. And it’s not just socks. Guests may be embarrassed by foot odor, lack of a pedicure, a medical condition or just weird-looking toes. (It’s my personal opinion that all toes are weird-looking, but whatever.)

Also, some people build their whole outfit around their shoes, and I am occasionally that person. A cute summer dress just isn’t as cute without the strappy heels, right? Asking someone to remove their shoes messes up the whole look—which isn’t a big deal for a casual visit but can be an issue if you’re meeting your son’s girlfriend’s parents for the first time.

As for the germs? Mopping isn’t really that hard. I hate it, but on the list of terrible chores, it’s not as awful as cleaning the toilet and maybe around the same level of annoying as wiping fingerprints off the stainless steel fridge. And it works: Mopping removes about 80% of tracked-in bacteria, while disinfecting gets rid of 95% to 99%, according to one study.

The gray areas

This isn’t solely (ha!) a cut-and-dry issue. And the more I think about it, the more middle ground I find. Here’s what to consider before setting a “shoes off” policy in your house.

  • The event. Asking a casual visitor to take off their shoes is fine. Asking someone who came over for a formal party or a holiday celebration may be rude because you wouldn’t take off your shoes if the party were held anywhere else.
  • The person. Some folks genuinely need to keep their shoes on, whether that’s for balance, mobility or a medical condition. You should never ask your guests to do something that could inconvenience or hurt them.
  • The time of year. While I still think shoes are dirty year-round, they are decidedly dirtier when it’s wet or snowy outside. There’s a huge difference between summer flip-flops and winter boots.
  • The way you ask. Some people have a cute sign by their door, others mention it as guests enter, and a fastidious few will communicate the instruction in advance. But you should have a plan, because verbally ambushing someone once they’re halfway into your home is not nice. However you ask, you should be polite, kind and willing to take no for an answer.
  • The method. Some cultures offer indoor slippers or shoe covers to guests, which is a lovely idea. While that’s not common in America, you can do things to make it more comfortable for your guests to remove their shoes, including having a bench where they can sit down and a mat or rack where they can place their shoes. Many of my Minnesota friends had a basket of clean guest socks by the front door.

What to do if someone refuses to take off their shoes

You accept it. Ultimately, it’s their body. This is not the hill to die on: In the grand scheme of things, this is small stakes. This is how you keep friends. This is also how I’m still married.

The verdict

It is not rude to ask someone to take off their shoes in your home—as long as you ask politely, offer options, are mindful of the situation and are ready to accept “no” as an answer. It doesn’t mean you have to be thrilled about it. And you are welcome to think vengeful thoughts as you mop the floor for the third time as your husband sits on the couch with his hiking shoes on, eating popcorn and smugly enjoying his shoe-wearing victory.

Why trust us

Reader’s Digest has published hundreds of etiquette stories that help readers navigate communication in a changing world. We regularly cover topics such as the best messages to send for any occasion, polite habits that aren’t as polite as they seem, email and texting etiquette, business etiquette, tipping etiquette, travel etiquette and more. We’re committed to producing high-quality content by writers with expertise and experience in their field in consultation with relevant, qualified experts. We rely on reputable primary sources, including government and professional organizations and academic institutions as well as our writers’ personal experiences where appropriate. We verify all facts and data, back them with credible sourcing and revisit them over time to ensure they remain accurate and up to date. Read more about our team, our contributors and our editorial policies.

articles.title: Here’s What Will Happen to Prince George, Prince Louis and Princess Charlotte’s Titles When William Becomes King
articles.content:
Queen Elizabeth II lived to the age of 96, and Prince Philip lived to 99, so it’s likely that 77-year-old King Charles III will be king for a good, long while. Still, Charles’s reign did not begin until he was 74, making him the longest-waiting heir and the oldest heir to become monarch, so his reign will not be a long one.
Charles’s son, Prince William, will eventually ascend the throne, and that one tiny shift is of great importance: It will cause a dramatic cascading effect when it comes to his kids’ titles, and beyond. “When a new monarch succeeds to the throne, the other members of the royal family move up in the line of succession,” says royal historian Carolyn Harris, PhD, author of Raising Royalty: 1,000 Years of Royal Parenting. But the royals’ new titles might not be as straightforward as you think. Plus, there might be a few historic firsts in store for Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis.
Read on to find out how William’s shift in status will affect his children, along with the ripple effect it could have on the rest of the monarchy.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more royals, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
Once William becomes king, the order of succession will largely remain the same—everyone will simply move up a spot. For example, Prince George, who is currently second in line, will become first in line, taking his father’s current title as Prince of Wales, which he acquired in 2022 after the queen died and Charles became king.
Succession always follows the monarch’s direct line, until there are no more direct descendants. At that point, it goes back up to the monarch’s younger sibling and his or her children. Therefore, William’s younger brother, Prince Harry, is in line behind George, Charlotte and Louis.
What’s more, Charlotte is the first female to be ahead of a younger brother in the line of succession. Charlotte, who would have previously been passed over for Louis, gets to keep her position in line thanks to the Succession to the Crown Act of 2013, enacted during Queen Elizabeth II’s reign. The law ended male primogeniture, or the tradition of the crown passing to the oldest male, for those born after 2011. Now, elder daughters are not left out and can inherit the crown as well.
Here’s the order of succession under a hypothetical King William:
As noted above, succession follows the direct descendants of each royal before passing to the royal’s younger sibling. That means each new royal child born bumps those in line after them back further, as evidenced by Princess Eugenie’s new royal baby, Adelaide, jumping in line ahead of Eugenie’s uncle, Prince Edward. Prince William’s children are likewise ahead of his younger brother, Prince Harry, who will keep getting pushed back as the Wales kids have their own children.
“There are numerous examples of members of the monarch’s family who were born close to the top of the line of succession who gradually dropped to a lower place in line as the royal extended family expanded over time,” Harris says. “For example, Queen Elizabeth II’s eldest cousin, George Lascelles, Earl of Harewood (1923–2011), was born sixth in line to the throne but was 46th in line to the throne at the time of his death.”
Princess Anne, the second child of Queen Elizabeth II, was born before the Succession to the Crown Act went into effect, so she remains far down on the list, behind younger brothers Andrew and Edward and their children.
Royal titles are both inherited and bestowed according to tradition. “According to letters patent issued by King George V in 1917, children and male-line grandchildren of the monarch hold the title of HRH Prince or Princess from birth,” Harris says. “It’s possible that in future reigns, these titles will be restricted to the children of the monarch and heir to the throne.” This would be in keeping with the recent paring down and streamlining of the monarchy.
In addition, princes and princesses can hold multiple titles such as duke, duchess or earl, which makes titles very confusing. Generally, the higher up the ranks you are, the more titles you end up with, and there is no official limit.
For example, Prince William holds three dukedoms: On William’s wedding day (a traditional title-giving day), Queen Elizabeth named him Duke of Cambridge, as well as Earl of Strathearn and Baron Carrickfergus. Then William inherited the titles of Duke of Cornwall and Duke of Rothesay when his father became king.
“The tradition of all the sons of the monarch receiving ducal titles dates from the reign of King Edward III (1327–1377), who had five sons who survived to adulthood,” Harris says. “Edward III made his eldest son and heir Prince Edward, Duke of Cornwall, so that he would have his own independent income. Younger sons received their own dukedoms (Clarence, Lancaster, York and Gloucester); the descendants of the Dukes of Lancaster and York would fight one another for the throne in the Wars of the Roses (1455–1487).”
Today, the title of Duke of Lancaster belongs to the monarch (whether male or female), and the title of Duke of York is traditionally given to the monarch’s second son. Prince Harry could not become Duke of York when he married Meghan in 2018, however, because the title was already held by his uncle, Andrew. Queen Elizabeth chose from available dukedoms for Harry, landing on Sussex, which was held only once before, by Prince Augustus Frederick in 1801. Meghan, however, is the first Duchess of Sussex because neither of Augustus’s marriages were approved by the crown. Augustus was considered progressive and somewhat of a rebel, like Harry, but the queen could not have known that Harry would become estranged from his father, as Augustus did because of his liberal views.
In addition to royal titles, William may also bestow some patronages. When there is a change in reign, there are often changes to royal patronages, as the late monarch’s patronages are redistributed to other members of the royal family.
“How this redistribution of patronages unfolds depends on the interests of individual members of the royal family and the overall approach to philanthropy in the new reign,” Harris says. “While Queen Elizabeth II and Charles III supported a broad range of different philanthropic organizations, William is focused on a smaller range of targeted issues, including the environment and alleviating homelessness.”
As the next heir apparent, Prince George will have the most changes to his titles. “The heir to the throne automatically becomes Duke of Cornwall and enjoys access to the revenues from the Duchy of Cornwall, and will receive the title of Prince of Wales from the monarch,” Harris says. The dukedom will provide George with an income and increase his wealth, as it did for William.
“William will decide when George becomes Prince of Wales, and William and George together will decide if a formal investiture as Prince of Wales will take place,” Harris says. For example, Charles was given the title Prince of Wales by Queen Elizabeth when he was 9 years old, six years after she became queen, but he did not have a formal ceremony (investiture) until he was 20.
The Prince of Wales title, while not guaranteed because it is given, not inherited, is almost a certainty because it is the usual title of the first male in line to the throne. Why? In 1301, after he had conquered Wales, King Edward I gave the title to his eldest son, Prince Edward; eventually, it became tradition. Upon taking the throne, Charles gave his former title Prince of Wales to William, who will almost certainly give it to George.
Princess Charlotte’s title may change, but not right away. “The eldest daughter of the monarch traditionally holds the title of Princess Royal,” Harris says. This title is not automatic; it is bestowed by the monarch. However, it is given for life, so Charlotte can’t have the title right away because there already is one: Princess Anne, Charles’s sister.
(Note that the future Queen Elizabeth II couldn’t be named Princess Royal because the title was already occupied by her aunt, Princess Mary, until well after Elizabeth became queen. And the queen’s sister, Princess Margaret, was never Princess Royal because she was the second-born daughter.)
“Only one Princess Royal exists at any one time, so Princess Charlotte will not receive this title until after the death of Princess Anne,” Harris says. At that point, the current monarch, who will probably be King Charles or the future King William, will likely give the title Princess Royal to Charlotte.
Another title reportedly intended for Charlotte (and potentially her future husband) is Duchess of Edinburgh, a title given to then–Princess Elizabeth upon her marriage to Prince Philip, who was styled as the Duke of Edinburgh. However, both titles are currently held by Prince Edward, Queen Elizabeth’s youngest son, and his wife, Sophie.
And, as mentioned earlier, Charlotte will not lose her place in line to the throne, since either sons or daughters can now inherit the crown.
Prince Louis’s title will remain the same, as will his place in line. He might get additional titles when William is king, but only after he’s an adult. “Prince Louis will likely receive a ducal title when he marries, as was the case for both Prince William and Prince Harry,” Harris says. However, any dukedom Louis receives is purely decorative and would not generate income. (The only profitable duchies today are Cornwall and Lancaster.)
Traditionally, the monarch gives the second son the title Duke of York, which is available now that Prince Andrew has had it taken away due to his criminal associations. The question is, however, whether it will still be too soon to use that title again due to its now-negative connotations.
Instead, Louis could be given a historic duchy title that has not been held for a long time, such as Clarence (although that one is said to be cursed) or Cambridge (which will revert to the crown when William becomes king). It’s also possible that by the time Louis is ready, the royal scandal with the last Duke of York might have faded, and Louis will hold the title after all, as per tradition.
This will likely be way in the future, but there are some things we know. “When George, Charlotte and Louis have children of their own, these children will take precedence over Prince Harry and his children in the line of succession,” Harris says. “Prince George’s eldest child, male or female, will become heir to the throne when George succeeds to the throne.”
If future King George’s eldest child is a daughter, regardless of whether he also has sons, she will make history as the first female heir apparent after the 2013 Succession to the Crown Act was passed. However, the act doesn’t apply to other inherited or traditionally gifted titles (yet), and it’s not clear exactly how getting rid of male primogeniture will affect them.
“If Prince George’s first child is a daughter, she may become the first princess to succeed to the Duchy of Cornwall as heir to the throne, which was previously reserved for male heirs to the throne,” Harris says. “The future Queen Elizabeth II did not have access to the revenues from the Duchy of Cornwall.”
In addition, if King George’s heir is a daughter, will she be given the title of Princess of Wales in place of Prince of Wales (provided the current Princess of Wales, Catherine, has vacated the title by becoming queen)? It’s possible. Chances are, new rules will be passed by then that will clarify these questions.
Only time will tell!

articles.title: Here’s What It Means If You See a Blue Traffic Light
articles.content:
Show almost anyone in the world a red, yellow and green light, and they’ll instantly associate the colorful trio with a traffic signal. But add another color to the mix, and many will be left in the dark—or, let’s be honest, totally and completely confused—about what it’s supposed to mean.
That’s exactly what’s happening in some parts of the United States: Drivers have spotted the addition of a bright blue light mounted near traffic signals. Yes, blue. But what is its purpose, and does it change how you should approach the intersection? Because remember: Just because you don’t know a traffic rule, it doesn’t mean you can’t get a ticket for it!
To get us all up to speed on this new rule of the road, Reader’s Digest spoke with David A. Noyce, executive associate dean of the College of Engineering and the Arthur F. Hawnn Professor of Transportation Engineering at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Read on to find out what those little blue lights mean—and what you should do when you see one.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, common curiosities, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
A blue light—often called a confirmation light or red-signal indicator—is designed to help law enforcement monitor, from a distance, whether the traffic signal is displaying a red light. Yep, its whole purpose is to let a copper know if someone’s run a red.
In case you’ve never seen one of these yourself, it’s not an extra circle in the red, yellow, green lineup. The blue light will typically be mounted above the traffic signal or, in some cases, higher up or to the side on the overhead mast arms.
What do these blue lights mean?

These blue lights are electrically linked to red lights on one or more of the approaches to the intersection. “Police use them to ‘observe’ the red light when they cannot see the actual red light directly,” Noyce explains. “Therefore, when the red-light traffic signal indication is illuminated, so is the blue light.”
Here’s the benefit: At signals without a blue light, an officer often has to be positioned near the same side of the intersection as a driver to confirm that they’ve run a red light. With a blue confirmation light, officers positioned at different angles or whose views are partially obstructed, perhaps by a tree branch, can verify that a signal is red by looking for the lit blue light, making it easier to spot drivers who fail to stop. Plus, it’s more efficient, since you need fewer officers to keep their eyes on the same stretch of road.
“The confirmation light is used to support a traffic law common in many states that requires a police officer to physically witness a violation to issue a citation,” Noyce says. “With the blue confirmation light, the police officer can physically witness red-light-running from anywhere in the intersection.”
Plus, according to a Federal Highway Administration research and technology report, these lights reduce the need for officers to cross the intersection against a red to pursue a driver who has run the signal. That makes the situation a whole lot safer for officers.
While nobody likes getting a ticket, better enforcement of red-light violations can prevent future crashes by identifying and stopping drivers who repeatedly blow through red lights as well as make others tempted to do the same think twice. And that can save lives—not only those behind the wheel and their passengers, but pedestrians and bicyclists too. According to the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, more than 141,000 people were injured in red-light-running crashes in 2024, and 1,119 were killed. Of the fatalities, about half were pedestrians, bicyclists or occupants of vehicles struck by drivers who ran reds.
Partly to avoid sending mixed signals. The Federal Highway Administration’s Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices advises that these lights “should be designed such that they do not confuse drivers,” meaning “they should not be red, yellow or green.” And since blue is not recognized as a standard traffic signal indication, Noyce notes that drivers are less likely to mistake it for a signal telling them to stop, slow down or go.
Plus, he adds, blue LEDs are relatively uncommon in the roadway environment and produce a highly visible and saturated light that stands out against the glow of headlights, streetlights and other signs, which tend to fall in the white, yellow, amber and red portions of the spectrum during the evening hours. Blue also has a strong association with law enforcement, reinforcing its purpose.
There’s no national database tracking where blue lights have been installed in the U.S., and they’re not part of the federal standard traffic signal system. As a result, confirmation-light usage is scattered, at best, and remains a locally adopted enforcement tool rather than a coordinated national practice, similar to blue stop signs. Since blue lights are not mandated by the federal government, local police departments and transportation agencies are usually the ones that decide to give them a try.
Based on his research and experience, Noyce says blue lights are most prevalent in Florida and Colorado, though they’ve also appeared in a handful of other states. In Minnesota, for example, the city of Maplewood installed the lights, and other communities followed, after the state’s Department of Transportation launched a formal safety study of Florida’s confirmation-light system and its effectiveness in 2014. That study found that crashes caused by red-light runners dropped by 33%.
And while social media may make blue lights seem like a newfound law-enforcement gadget, these devices have actually been around for years. They were reportedly in use as early as 2007 in Marysville, Washington. In general, though, because the devices are often installed in one intersection at a time—and not uniformly citywide—they tend to receive only sporadic local-news coverage.
The same thing you always do: Obey the normal traffic rules. It’s not there to convey anything to you—it’s strictly for police officers. (That said, blue-confirmation lights don’t necessarily indicate a cop is around.)
For the average driver, bicyclist or pedestrian, they “mean nothing from a ‘rules of the road’ standpoint,” Noyce says. “But, perhaps, some drivers will react differently by deciding not to run a red light when in other instances they may have considered it.”

That’s exactly what’s happening in some parts of the United States: Drivers have spotted the addition of a bright blue light mounted near traffic signals. Yes, blue. But what is its purpose, and does it change how you should approach the intersection? Because remember: Just because you don’t know a traffic rule, it doesn’t mean you can’t get a ticket for it!

To get us all up to speed on this new rule of the road, Reader’s Digest spoke with David A. Noyce, executive associate dean of the College of Engineering and the Arthur F. Hawnn Professor of Transportation Engineering at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Read on to find out what those little blue lights mean—and what you should do when you see one.
